strengths: The paper offers a potentially useful combination of BORE-style classification with graph-based semi-supervised learning. Supporting both fixed candidate pools and generated unlabeled points makes the approach applicable to several optimization settings, and its relationship to BORE and LFBO is explained clearly.

The experiments show promising improvements, particularly on synthetic functions and NATS-Bench, against multiple classifier-based methods and GP baselines. Reporting 20 repetitions with standard errors provides useful evidence beyond individual successful runs.

The appendices investigate bandwidth, sampling distributions, unlabeled sample counts, pool subsampling, and threshold ratios. These studies expose meaningful sensitivities and computational limitations.
weaknesses: The central explanation for improved exploration is insufficiently established. Sampling truncated Gaussians around previous queries does not ensure that high-density regions align with the changing good/bad objective labels required by Assumption 4.1. Appendix C appropriately acknowledges that the cited i.i.d. classification guarantees do not apply to adaptive BO. Enlarging the high-probability region alone therefore does not establish a better exploration–exploitation balance.

The experiments do not convincingly isolate the benefit of unlabeled propagation. Figure 12 includes a valuable no-transductive baseline, but uses fixed beta = 0.5, whereas the main results learn substantially different bandwidths. The ablation also contains cases where removing unlabeled data improves performance. Comparably tuned supervised kernel baselines and controls for bandwidth adaptation and random tie-breaking are needed to substantiate the principal contribution.

Although the baseline suite includes the main BORE/LFBO methods, it omits random search and simple versions with explicit exploration, which are especially relevant to the claimed remedy for over-exploitation. This issue is already recognized in the cited literature, making these comparisons important for establishing the new method's significance. Continuous-domain evaluation is also limited to four two-dimensional functions.

The MNIST experiment provides limited evidence of general high-dimensional black-box optimization. Appendix D.5 trains the encoder on 440,000 labeled images to predict the same 1,000 three-digit classes whose numerical values are subsequently minimized. The separate test split avoids direct test-label leakage, but this supplies substantial objective-specific supervision. Ranking candidates using the pretrained classifier is an essential missing baseline.

Several details needed for reproduction remain unspecified: input scaling, the label-spreading clamping factor, propagation stopping settings, bandwidth initialization and bounds, and acquisition maximization over finite pools. The L-BFGS-B description does not resolve the latter or explain baseline acquisition-search procedures. A smaller mathematical correction is also needed: the elementwise column-normalized definition of P conflicts with the stated matrix expression P = D^{-1}W.

The computational assessment only varies subset size within the proposed method. It does not compare end-to-end overhead or optimization performance against elapsed time for the baselines. Repeated graph construction, bandwidth optimization, and 1,000 acquisition-search initializations make this a meaningful unresolved practical tradeoff.
